metadata.note: The Rio Grande Southern Railroad (RGS) was a 3-foot narrow-gauge line through the San Juan Mountains of southwestern Colorado, running Durango-Mancos-Hesperus-Dolores-Rico-Lizard Head Pass-Ophir-Vance Junction-Placerville-Dallas Divide-Ridgway (162 miles), with a 10-mile branch from Vance Junction up the San Miguel River valley to Telluride (172 route-miles total). Incorporated November 5 1889 by Otto Mears, built by Denver & Rio Grande interests but chartered and operated as its own separate company; the D&RG became its controlling creditor after an 1893-95 receivership (roughly 70% ownership via loans/notes) and D&RG/D&RGW remained the controlling stockholder for the rest of the RGS's existence, but the RGS was never absorbed, merged or renamed -- it stayed a legally distinct company through its own separate 1929 bankruptcy and all the way to its 1951-52 abandonment. Per this project's one-company-one-color rule this map therefore keeps the RGS as a single company with a single color across its whole existence (no split at 1893 or 1929: the controlling entity tightened its grip on RGS finances at those dates, but the operating company itself never changed hands to a genuinely different owner the way, e.g., the Ulster & Delaware or Watertown & Rome did) -- and keeps that color visually distinct from the browns/rust-oranges used elsewhere in this dataset for the Denver & Rio Grande Railway (#8B5E3C) and the Denver and Rio Grande Western Railroad (#B5451B), since the RGS is a genuinely separate company under this project's rules. Famous for the 'Galloping Goose' motor railcars (self-built from automobile parts starting 1931) that kept its mail contract, and hence its passenger service, alive through the Depression after conventional steam trains became too costly. Passenger/mail service wound down from regular daily runs (ended Dec 18 1949) to summer-only tourist excursions (1950-51, still passenger service under this project's rules) before the railroad suspended all operations December 17 1951 and was formally abandoned in spring 1952.

geometry_sources: OpenStreetMap (via Overpass API, https://overpass-api.de/api/interpreter): railway=abandoned ways tagged name="Rio Grande Southern" or old_railway_operator=RGS across the Durango-Mancos-Dolores-Rico-Lizard Head Pass-Ophir-Vance Junction-Placerville-Ridgway corridor (37.15-38.25N, 108.6-107.55W). 35 usable way fragments (~171 km / ~106 mi of real-traced grade) were assembled with a haversine-Dijkstra router (nodes snapped to 5 decimals) and ordered along the route by projecting each fragment onto a waypoint reference line. One unnamed fragment (OSM way 99613846, FIXME 'Where was the north end?') was excluded: its shape is a tight switchback loop just north of Durango that does not track the mainline's westward Lightner Creek alignment there and is more consistent with the separate Boston Coal & Fuel Railroad spur (a freight-only coal branch, out of scope under this project's passenger-only rule) than with the RGS mainline; several 'Boston Coal & Fuel Railroad' / 'Twin Buttes Trail' / 'BC&F Road' -named ways in the same Durango-area cluster were excluded for the same reason. Ways explicitly named 'Rio Grande Southern (Chama to Durango)' with old_railway_operator=D&RGW were also excluded -- despite the RGS name in the OSM tag, that corridor is the separate D&RG/D&RGW San Juan Extension (Chama-Durango, today's Cumbres & Toltec/Durango & Silverton heritage lines), not this railroad.

Gaps with no matching OSM railway tagging (~78 km / ~48 mi, about 31% of the assembled route) are straight-line connectors between the nearest traced fragment ends and/or geocoded waypoints (Nominatim) for Durango, Hesperus, Mancos, Dolores, Rico, Lizard Head Pass, Ophir, Vance Junction, Placerville, Dallas Divide and Ridgway -- flagged, not guessed at higher precision.

Telluride Branch (Vance Junction-Telluride, ~10 documented miles): no OSM railway=abandoned/disused tagging was found for this branch specifically. Approximated using the modern CO-145/Colorado Avenue road corridor through the San Miguel River valley, which occupies the same narrow valley the branch is documented to have used; this is a road-corridor approximation, not a track-verified trace.
metadata.not_yet_sourced: Exact scheduled timetable/frequency for any era (headway_min values below are rough estimates for a lightly-trafficked narrow-gauge mountain branch, not sourced to a timetable). The formal ICC abandonment date has a one-source discrepancy: Wikipedia gives April 24 1952, American-Rails.com gives April 15 1952; both are given in the sources above rather than silently picking one. The Boston Coal & Fuel Railroad branch (a coal-mine spur near Durango) and the Mayday Mine branch are not traced on this map: freight-only branches are out of scope under this project's passenger-only rule (CLAUDE.md Rule 1), and no passenger service on either is documented.

properties.speed_source: estimated: narrow-gauge (3ft) mountain main line over Lizard Head Pass (grades to ~4%), Durango-Ridgway; steam-era mixed/passenger trains likely averaged nearer 15 km/h given the grades and 162-mile length, the lighter post-1931 Galloping Goose motors somewhat faster; no timetable located, unsourced

segments.note: Through service Durango-Ridgway began with the first complete 162-mile run on January 2 1892, following construction from both ends in 1890-91 by Otto Mears's Rio Grande Southern (incorporated Nov 5 1889). After the Panic of 1893 silver crash the RGS entered voluntary receivership (Aug 2 1893); the Denver & Rio Grande became its controlling creditor at roughly 70% ownership via loans and endorsed notes, and receivership ended Dec 1 1895 with the RGS continuing as a legally separate, D&RG-controlled company -- not merged or renamed, so this map keeps it as its own company/color per this project's convention rather than splitting or recoloring to the D&RG. Conventional steam-hauled mixed and passenger trains ran throughout this era; frequency estimated (roughly a daily mixed train) and unsourced.

segments.note: The RGS entered its own receivership/bankruptcy on December 11 1929 (separate from, and roughly seven years after, the Denver & Rio Grande Western's 1922 bankruptcy) as Depression-era traffic collapsed; the D&RGW showed little interest in propping up the money-losing branch. Conventional steam service continued under receiver management until the first Galloping Goose motor entered service in 1931. Frequency estimated, unsourced.

segments.note: Chief mechanic-built Galloping Goose motor railcars (improvised from automobile parts) began replacing costly steam passenger trains: Motor #1 first ran June 1 1931, the first true boxcab 'Goose' (#2) on August 12 1931, and by 1933 the Geese were hauling most of the line's passengers, mail and light freight. Regularly scheduled mail-and-passenger service continued, latterly almost entirely by Goose, until it lapsed on December 18 1949 as winter weather stopped regular runs. Frequency estimated (roughly a daily mixed run), unsourced.

segments.note: The federal government did not renew the RGS's US Mail contract in 1950, ending the line's main revenue source. The railroad kept a skeleton of passenger service alive as a summer tourist excursion operation -- Goose express compartments were converted for sightseeing passengers in spring 1950 -- running in the summers of 1950 and 1951; this tourist/excursion service still counts as passenger service under this project's rules. It did not generate enough revenue to save the railroad: operations were suspended December 17 1951, the ICC approved abandonment the following spring (sources differ: April 15 1952 per American-Rails.com, April 24 1952 per Wikipedia), and the track was scrapped by March 1953. Frequency estimated as a seasonal weekly-ish excursion schedule, unsourced.

properties.geometry_source: OpenStreetMap Overpass (railway=abandoned, name/old_railway_operator=Rio Grande Southern/RGS), Dijkstra-routed and gap-connected; see metadata.geometry_sources for the full method and exclusions.
properties.geometry_quality: Mixed real-traced and flagged-approximate. Of the assembled ~248.9 km (~154.7 mi) mainline path, ~171.0 km (~106.3 mi, ~68.7%) is real-traced from OpenStreetMap abandoned-railway tagging specific to the Rio Grande Southern; ~77.9 km (~48.4 mi, ~31.3%) is straight-line connectors across gaps where no matching OSM track/trail geometry survives (largely west and northwest of Durango toward Hesperus/Mancos, and several short gaps in the Dolores River canyon and near Rico/Lizard Head Pass/Ophir). This traced length is somewhat short of the documented 162-mile main line (154.7 mi assembled vs 162 mi documented) because the router takes the shortest connected path through each OSM fragment and the straight-line gap connectors cut corners on some of the line's real curves and switchbacks -- so this geometry understates the true sinuosity/mileage in the gapped stretches. Tight hairpin/switchback-shaped curves survive in the traced portions near Mancos/Dolores and, notably, around Ophir (~37.86N,-107.88W) -- consistent with the well-documented 'Ophir Loop' where the line spiraled to gain elevation -- and were checked point-by-point (cumulative along-path distance vs direct distance) to confirm they are continuous, non-repeating traces and not a routing artifact; one genuine artifact (a looping, unnamed OSM fragment near Durango, way 99613846, likely the freight-only Boston Coal & Fuel spur) was found and excluded rather than included as if it were the passenger mainline.

properties.speed_source: estimated: narrow-gauge branch, San Miguel River valley, Vance Junction-Telluride; unsourced

segments.note: The ~10-mile branch from Vance Junction (on the RGS main line) up the San Miguel River valley to Telluride was part of the RGS's original construction and opened ahead of the Durango-Ridgway through connection, completed November 23 1890. It shared the main line's corporate and passenger history thereafter -- see the Durango-Ridgway feature's segment notes for the 1893-95 receivership, the 1929 RGS bankruptcy, the 1931 introduction of the Galloping Goose motors, and the 1949-51 wind-down to summer tourist excursions before operations were suspended December 17 1951. Frequency estimated, unsourced.

properties.geometry_source: Modern CO-145/Colorado Avenue road corridor (OpenStreetMap), approximating the historic San Miguel River valley alignment; see metadata.geometry_sources.
properties.geometry_quality: Straight-line/road-corridor approximation, not track-verified. No OpenStreetMap railway=abandoned or disused tagging was found for this branch specifically (unlike the main line, which has extensive 'Rio Grande Southern'-tagged fragments). This feature instead follows the modern CO-145 highway and Colorado Avenue through the same narrow San Miguel River valley the branch is documented to have used between Vance Junction and Telluride, a corridor with little room for the road and the old grade to have diverged significantly, but this is an approximation and should be labelled as such rather than presented as a real trace. Length as drawn is approximately 13 km (~8 mi), short of the documented 10-mile (~16 km) branch mileage, since the road takes a more direct line through the valley than the railroad's easier-graded curves would have.
